entries.q: Do CPA firms need client consent to use offshore staff?
entries.a: Yes, if tax return information will be disclosed to anyone located outside the United States. The rule applies to the firm's own employees abroad as well as to outside providers, and consent must be signed before the first disclosure.
entries.t: Section 7216 Consent for Offshore Staff: What CPA Firms Need in Place Before Busy Season

entries.q: Can a tax firm send Social Security numbers to an offshore team?
entries.a: Only with the client's consent and only if both the US firm and the offshore recipient maintain an adequate data protection safeguard as defined in Rev. Proc. 2013-14. Otherwise the SSN must be masked or redacted before the information leaves the United States.
entries.t: Section 7216 Consent for Offshore Staff: What CPA Firms Need in Place Before Busy Season

entries.q: How long does a Section 7216 consent last?
entries.a: As long as the form states. Where no duration is given, consent lapses one year after the client signed.
entries.t: Section 7216 Consent for Offshore Staff: What CPA Firms Need in Place Before Busy Season

entries.q: Can Section 7216 consent be signed electronically?
entries.a: Yes. The client must affirmatively enter a PIN of at least five characters, type their own name, or enter five or more characters unique to them, and the software may not pre-fill the signature.
entries.t: Section 7216 Consent for Offshore Staff: What CPA Firms Need in Place Before Busy Season

entries.q: What is the penalty for disclosing tax return information without consent?
entries.a: Civil penalties start at $250 per disclosure, up to $10,000 a year, rising to $1,000 and $50,000 where the disclosure relates to identity theft. A knowing or reckless disclosure is also a misdemeanour carrying a fine and up to one year in prison.
entries.t: Section 7216 Consent for Offshore Staff: What CPA Firms Need in Place Before Busy Season

entries.q: What are the stages of AI adoption in finance teams?
entries.a: A common model has three: curious, where people use AI tools individually; connected, where at least one finance process has been changed with AI integrated into the systems; and compounding, where a whole function has been redesigned around AI.
entries.t: Curious, Connected, Compounding: AI Adoption in Finance Teams

entries.q: Where are most finance teams with AI today?
entries.a: Most are at the curious stage, using tools individually without changing processes. In rooms of finance leaders in late 2026, few described themselves as connected and very few as compounding.
entries.t: Curious, Connected, Compounding: AI Adoption in Finance Teams

entries.q: Why do AI projects in finance fail?
entries.a: Mostly at adoption rather than build. The tool works, but people keep the old process, time savings are absorbed rather than reinvested, and nobody owns the change. Starting with people and process before tooling avoids most of this.
entries.t: Curious, Connected, Compounding: AI Adoption in Finance Teams

entries.q: Should AI agents have direct access to accounting data?
entries.a: Only with controls in place first: authentication at the data layer, permissions limited to what the agent needs, a log of its actions, and human review of anything posted to the ledger. Read-only analysis and write access are different risks.
entries.t: Curious, Connected, Compounding: AI Adoption in Finance Teams

entries.q: How should a CFO start an AI rollout in finance?
entries.a: Pick one process, agree how it should work, find the people already getting results, write a short AI use policy, and move to the next process only when the first is working and trusted.
entries.t: Curious, Connected, Compounding: AI Adoption in Finance Teams

entries.q: Why is the finance talent pipeline under pressure?
entries.a: Two things are happening at once. Experienced CFOs are retiring at a high rate, and AI is taking over the routine work junior finance staff used to learn on, which reduces the repetitions that build judgment.
entries.t: The Finance Talent Pipeline After AI: Who Learns to Catch the Errors?

entries.q: Are CFOs retiring in record numbers?
entries.a: As a share of departures, yes. Russell Reynolds found retirements and moves to board roles were 61% of global CFO departures in the first three quarters of 2026, the highest in its eight-year series. The overall departure rate was steady at 12%.
entries.t: The Finance Talent Pipeline After AI: Who Learns to Catch the Errors?

entries.q: What is the average tenure of a CFO?
entries.a: Crist|Kolder puts average tenure for sitting CFOs at Fortune 500 and S&P 500 companies at 4.5 years, and Spencer Stuart reports 4.7 years for S&P 500 CFOs. Claims that tenure is under three years are not supported by the published data.
entries.t: The Finance Talent Pipeline After AI: Who Learns to Catch the Errors?

entries.q: Should finance teams still hire junior analysts if AI can do the work?
entries.a: Most CFOs say yes, but fewer and differently. Someone has to check AI output and grow into senior roles, which needs hands-on experience and a combination of curiosity and drive.
entries.t: The Finance Talent Pipeline After AI: Who Learns to Catch the Errors?

entries.q: How can finance leaders develop junior staff when AI does the routine work?
entries.a: Keep some work deliberately manual, review AI output together with the junior who submitted it, decide where saved time goes, and rotate juniors through different parts of the function.
entries.t: The Finance Talent Pipeline After AI: Who Learns to Catch the Errors?

entries.q: What interview questions reveal drive in a finance candidate?
entries.a: Ask the candidate to describe something they taught themselves and applied at work without being asked, and what it changed. A specific, recent example with a visible result is the signal. A training course the employer arranged is not.
entries.t: Finance Interview Questions That Test for Drive and Coachability

entries.q: How do you test coachability in an interview?
entries.a: Ask about the last piece of tough feedback the candidate received and what they did with it. A coachable candidate states the feedback plainly, says what was fair in it and describes a change. Explaining why the reviewer was wrong is a red flag.
entries.t: Finance Interview Questions That Test for Drive and Coachability

entries.q: Is intellectual curiosity enough when hiring for finance roles?
entries.a: No. Curiosity needs to be paired with drive, the habit of learning without being asked and applying it. Curious people without drive tend to be interested in problems without moving them forward.
entries.t: Finance Interview Questions That Test for Drive and Coachability

entries.q: Why do drive and coachability matter more because of AI?
entries.a: AI now does much of the routine work that junior finance staff used to learn from. People who seek out understanding on their own, and who accept correction, are better placed to catch AI errors and build judgment without those repetitions.
entries.t: Finance Interview Questions That Test for Drive and Coachability

entries.q: Should these questions replace technical interviews for accountants and FP&A analysts?
entries.a: No. Keep the technical screen to test whether the candidate can do the work today. These questions test whether they will keep improving, and they work best alongside it.
entries.t: Finance Interview Questions That Test for Drive and Coachability

entries.q: What is the main risk of using AI in finance?
entries.a: Confident, wrong output that nobody catches. AI presents a weak answer in the same polished form as a strong one, and people without enough experience may not notice the difference.
entries.t: AI in Finance Has a Confidence Problem, Not a Speed Problem

entries.q: How much time do finance teams spend checking AI output?
entries.a: In Datarails' 2026 survey of 270 US CFOs and finance leaders, finance teams reported spending 26% of their working week verifying or correcting AI output. Workday's 2026 research found nearly 40% of AI time savings were lost to fixing low-quality output. Both are self-reported.
entries.t: AI in Finance Has a Confidence Problem, Not a Speed Problem

entries.q: Can one AI agent check another's financial work?
entries.a: It can catch some errors, especially formula and consistency mistakes, but it does not replace a finance expert. Both agents can miss the same thing, such as a term in a loan agreement that never made it into the model.
entries.t: AI in Finance Has a Confidence Problem, Not a Speed Problem

entries.q: How should finance teams review AI-generated models?
entries.a: Assign a named reviewer, tie every schedule back to source documents and the ledger, check the terms that drive the numbers most, and track how much time verification takes.
entries.t: AI in Finance Has a Confidence Problem, Not a Speed Problem

entries.q: What is the Dunning–Kruger effect and why does it matter for AI?
entries.a: It is the finding, from Kruger and Dunning's 1999 studies, that people with the least skill tend to overestimate their performance most. Researchers still debate how much of it is a statistical artefact. For AI, the practical point is that the people most able to produce work beyond their experience are the least able to check it.
entries.t: AI in Finance Has a Confidence Problem, Not a Speed Problem

entries.q: What are the different types of CFO?
entries.a: A useful split is architect, builder and foreman. The architect designs the finance function, the builder implements it, and the foreman runs and improves it. Most CFOs are strongest in one or two of the three.
entries.t: Architect, Builder or Foreman: The Three Types of CFO and Which One You Need

entries.q: Which type of CFO does a growing company need?
entries.a: A company outgrowing its first finance hire usually needs a builder to put in systems, a reliable close and the first team. Before that, a part-time architect is often enough. Once the function is in place, a foreman keeps it running and improving.
entries.t: Architect, Builder or Foreman: The Three Types of CFO and Which One You Need

entries.q: Does a private equity-backed company need a different CFO at different stages?
entries.a: Often, yes. Early in a hold period the priority is bringing reporting and controls up to the sponsor's standard, which suits a builder. The middle years reward a foreman, and exit preparation calls for architect work again.
entries.t: Architect, Builder or Foreman: The Three Types of CFO and Which One You Need

entries.q: Can one CFO be architect, builder and foreman?
entries.a: Occasionally, but rarely at the same time. The roles need different distance from the detail and different amounts of time. It is usually better to hire for the stage ahead and cover the other roles with advisers or the team below the CFO.
entries.t: Architect, Builder or Foreman: The Three Types of CFO and Which One You Need

entries.q: Why is influence important for a CFO?
entries.a: Because finance is now embedded in the operating teams rather than sitting apart, and most of the decisions that affect financial results are made by other leaders. A CFO's impact depends on whether those leaders seek out and act on the finance view.
entries.t: CFO Influence in 2027: Why the Reframer Wins

entries.q: How does a CFO build influence?
entries.a: Through time and trust. Time means being in the business and understanding the operating leaders' problems. Trust comes from being right, consistent and early with bad news. Lose either and influence falls away.
entries.t: CFO Influence in 2027: Why the Reframer Wins

entries.q: What does it mean for a CFO to be a reframer?
entries.a: A reframer moves stakeholders from what they ask for to what they need, and owns the narrative around a decision. Adaptability responds to change; reframing shapes how the change is understood.
entries.t: CFO Influence in 2027: Why the Reframer Wins

entries.q: What is the Claim, Check, Change exercise?
entries.a: A short self-assessment. Claim one skill for the coming year, check it against a specific example from the last 60 days and rate it, have a peer rate the same example, then decide on one change to strengthen the skill or build it in others.
entries.t: CFO Influence in 2027: Why the Reframer Wins

entries.q: Are soft skills more important than technical skills for CFOs?
entries.a: Technical skill is still the entry ticket, but it no longer decides success. Communication, change management and the ability to explain the numbers in the business's terms increasingly do, and CFOs describe them as the hardest skills to build.
entries.t: CFO Influence in 2027: Why the Reframer Wins

entries.q: What is AI in the office of the CFO?
entries.a: AI in the office of the CFO is the use of AI tools in the finance function's own work, such as payables, receivables, the close, reporting and compliance. In practice it means software that reads, classifies, matches and drafts, while people review, approve and remain accountable.
entries.t: AI in the Office of the CFO: A Practical Guide for 2027

entries.q: Where should a CFO start with AI?
entries.a: Start with one high-volume, rules-heavy process such as accounts payable exceptions or cash application. Measure the baseline first, give the tool read-only access to the existing system, agree the success measures and name a control owner before the pilot begins.
entries.t: AI in the Office of the CFO: A Practical Guide for 2027

entries.q: How many finance teams are using AI?
entries.a: Gartner's survey of 183 finance leaders, published in November 2025, found 59% using AI in their finance function. KPMG's 2026 survey of 1,013 senior finance leaders reported active use rising from 30% to 75% since 2024. The surveys use different samples and definitions.
entries.t: AI in the Office of the CFO: A Practical Guide for 2027

entries.q: Why do so few finance AI projects show a large impact?
entries.a: Usually because the pilot had no baseline, the process was not redesigned around the tool, or the team ran the old and new ways side by side. Gartner's June 2026 release reported only 7% of finance organizations seeing a high or very high impact.
entries.t: AI in the Office of the CFO: A Practical Guide for 2027

entries.q: Does AI in finance need new controls?
entries.a: Yes. Any AI-assisted step that affects financial reporting needs a defined review, logged evidence and controlled changes to prompts and rules. Discuss the design with your auditors before the step goes live.
entries.t: AI in the Office of the CFO: A Practical Guide for 2027

entries.q: Do we need to replace our ERP to use AI?
entries.a: No. Most of the value comes from a layer that reads from the existing ERP, shows exceptions and keeps a record, alongside the AI features the ERP vendor provides. The ERP remains the book of record.
entries.t: AI in the Office of the CFO: A Practical Guide for 2027

entries.q: When does SAP ECC mainstream maintenance end?
entries.a: SAP's Support Portal states that mainstream maintenance for SAP Business Suite 7 core applications, including SAP ERP 6.0, runs until the end of 2027.
entries.t: SAP ECC End of Maintenance: What 2027 Means for Finance Teams

entries.q: What is SAP extended maintenance and what does it cost?
entries.a: Extended maintenance is an optional period from the beginning of 2028 until the end of 2030, which SAP prices at a premium of two percentage points on the maintenance basis.
entries.t: SAP ECC End of Maintenance: What 2027 Means for Finance Teams

entries.q: Do the 2027 dates apply to every ECC system?
entries.a: Not necessarily in the same way. Check the releases and enhancement packages you run against SAP's maintenance page and your contract, because the dates apply to what SAP lists.
entries.t: SAP ECC End of Maintenance: What 2027 Means for Finance Teams

entries.q: What should finance do before an ECC migration?
entries.a: Write down the control objectives and exception owners independently of ECC, inventory the reports finance relies on, plan how open items will move, and keep go-live clear of year-end where possible.
entries.t: SAP ECC End of Maintenance: What 2027 Means for Finance Teams

entries.q: Can finance controls stay the same through a migration?
entries.a: The control objectives can stay the same, but their implementation changes. Each automated control has to be rebuilt and retested in the new system before it can be relied on.
entries.t: SAP ECC End of Maintenance: What 2027 Means for Finance Teams

entries.q: What should a new owner do with accounts payable after buying a business?
entries.a: List every open bill and mark which belong to the period before closing, clean the vendor list, verify vendor bank details, set approval rules and a regular payment run, tell key suppliers about the change of ownership, and then automate.
entries.t: Accounts Payable After an Acquisition: What to Fix First

entries.q: Who pays bills from before the closing date?
entries.a: Generally the seller, for goods and services received before closing, though the purchase agreement decides. These bills are usually settled through the post-closing working capital true-up.
entries.t: Accounts Payable After an Acquisition: What to Fix First

entries.q: How can a business prevent vendor payment fraud?
entries.a: Verify any new or changed vendor bank details by phone on a number already on file, never one provided in the request, and make it a rule that applies to everyone, including the owner.
entries.t: Accounts Payable After an Acquisition: What to Fix First

entries.q: When should accounts payable be automated after an acquisition?
entries.a: After the open bills are listed, the vendor list is clean, and approval rules and a payment rhythm are in place. Automating an unclear process makes it faster, not clearer.
entries.t: Accounts Payable After an Acquisition: What to Fix First

entries.q: What is the 1099 threshold for 2026?
entries.a: For payments made after 31 December 2025, most payments reported on Forms 1099-NEC and 1099-MISC are reportable only once they reach $2,000 in the calendar year, up from $600. Gross proceeds paid to attorneys are still reported from $600.
entries.t: Year-End Close for 2026: What Changes, Including the $2,000 1099 Threshold

entries.q: Do I need to issue a 1099 to a contractor I paid $1,500 in 2026?
entries.a: Generally no, for nonemployee compensation, because the 2026 threshold for Form 1099-NEC is $2,000. Check the IRS instructions for the specific type of payment, and keep the contractor's Form W-9 on file.
entries.t: Year-End Close for 2026: What Changes, Including the $2,000 1099 Threshold

entries.q: When are 1099s due in 2027?
entries.a: Forms 1099-NEC are due to recipients and the IRS by 31 January. Because 31 January 2027 is a Sunday, the deadline moves to Monday 1 February 2027.
entries.t: Year-End Close for 2026: What Changes, Including the $2,000 1099 Threshold

entries.q: Did the Form 1099-K threshold change?
entries.a: Yes. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act restored the earlier rule, so payment platforms are not required to issue Form 1099-K unless payments to a payee exceed $20,000 and there are more than 200 transactions.
entries.t: Year-End Close for 2026: What Changes, Including the $2,000 1099 Threshold

entries.q: What should a year-end close checklist include?
entries.a: Collecting Forms W-9, reconciling every account, reviewing receivables and revenue cut-off, accruing expenses and bonuses, counting inventory, reconciling payroll, locking the year in the accounting system and preparing a package for the CPA.
entries.t: Year-End Close for 2026: What Changes, Including the $2,000 1099 Threshold

entries.q: When should a business build its annual budget?
entries.a: Before the year starts. For a business on a calendar year, the budget for the following year is usually built in the last quarter, so hiring and spending decisions can be made in time.
entries.t: Your First Real Annual Budget: Building FY2027 for a $3–10M Services Business

entries.q: How do you budget revenue for a services business?
entries.a: Build it from committed client revenue, likely renewals and expansions, and weighted new pipeline, phased by when the work will start, then check it against the capacity of the delivery team.
entries.t: Your First Real Annual Budget: Building FY2027 for a $3–10M Services Business

entries.q: What is the difference between a budget and a forecast?
entries.a: A budget is a fixed plan set before the year begins. A forecast is updated during the year as results come in. Businesses usually keep the budget fixed for comparison and maintain a rolling forecast alongside it.
entries.t: Your First Real Annual Budget: Building FY2027 for a $3–10M Services Business

entries.q: Why does a budget need a cash budget as well as a profit budget?
entries.a: Because profit and cash arrive at different times. A business can be profitable for the year and still run short of cash in particular months, especially while it is growing and receivables rise.
entries.t: Your First Real Annual Budget: Building FY2027 for a $3–10M Services Business

entries.q: What should be reviewed each month against the budget?
entries.a: Revenue, gross margin, utilization, overhead, cash and receivables days, with a short written explanation for each significant difference from budget.
entries.t: Your First Real Annual Budget: Building FY2027 for a $3–10M Services Business

entries.q: What is job costing?
entries.a: Tracking the labor, materials, equipment and other direct costs of each job or customer against the revenue it earns, so the profitability of each one can be seen.
entries.t: Job Costing After an Acquisition: Finding Out Which Customers Make Money

entries.q: How do I find out which customers are profitable?
entries.a: Tie labor, including travel time, and purchases to customers or jobs, then compare each one's revenue with its direct costs. A rough first cut by area or service line can give useful answers before full job costing is in place.
entries.t: Job Costing After an Acquisition: Finding Out Which Customers Make Money

entries.q: What costs are most often missed in job costing?
entries.a: Drive time, small material purchases on cards, equipment wear and fuel, and callbacks or rework that earn no additional revenue.
entries.t: Job Costing After an Acquisition: Finding Out Which Customers Make Money

entries.q: What should I do with unprofitable customers?
entries.a: Reprice the work, change terms such as minimum visit sizes or travel charges, group the work into routes, or stop serving it if none of those make it pay.
entries.t: Job Costing After an Acquisition: Finding Out Which Customers Make Money

entries.q: What is the Profit First method?
entries.a: A cash management method from Mike Michalowicz's book Profit First, in which incoming money is divided across separate bank accounts for profit, owner's pay, tax and operating expenses on a fixed schedule, so profit is set aside before spending.
entries.t: Profit First or a Cash Forecast? What Each One Tells an Owner

entries.q: Does Profit First work for growing businesses?
entries.a: It provides useful discipline, but it does not show when large payments will fall. Growing businesses with uneven cash flow often add a forward cash forecast to time transfers and spot shortfalls.
entries.t: Profit First or a Cash Forecast? What Each One Tells an Owner

entries.q: What is the difference between Profit First and a cash flow forecast?
entries.a: Profit First allocates money already received. A cash flow forecast projects receipts and payments week by week, showing when cash will be short and how decisions would affect it.
entries.t: Profit First or a Cash Forecast? What Each One Tells an Owner

entries.q: Can I use Profit First and a cash forecast together?
entries.a: Yes. Keep the Profit First accounts for discipline and use the forecast to decide when to move money, so the operating account is funded before large payments fall due.
entries.t: Profit First or a Cash Forecast? What Each One Tells an Owner

entries.q: Why does working capital change during the month?
entries.a: Because billing, customer payments, payroll and supplier payments each happen on their own schedule. Receivables, payables and cash rise and fall through the month as each one occurs.
entries.t: Plan Working Capital Around the Peak, Not the Average

entries.q: What is peak working capital?
entries.a: The highest working capital requirement in a business's cycle, usually the point where it has paid out the most and collected the least. Cash and credit should be planned to cover it.
entries.t: Plan Working Capital Around the Peak, Not the Average

entries.q: How should a line of credit be sized?
entries.a: To cover the business's peak working capital need with a margin, and with terms that allow drawing and repaying within the cycle.
entries.t: Plan Working Capital Around the Peak, Not the Average

entries.q: How do I find when my working capital peaks?
entries.a: Map when you bill, when customers pay, when payroll runs and when suppliers are due, then measure receivables, payables and cash at each of those points over several months.
entries.t: Plan Working Capital Around the Peak, Not the Average

entries.q: Does the company keep its books after a stock purchase?
entries.a: Yes. In a stock purchase the company remains the same legal entity, so its existing books continue and the closing transactions are recorded in them.
entries.t: Your Books After a Stock Purchase: Recording the Deal Before the CPA Asks

entries.q: What should be recorded in the books after an acquisition?
entries.a: Debt paid off at closing, transaction costs that belong to the company, payouts to employees or the seller, any new loan borrowed by the company, amounts owed to or from the buyer's holding company, and the cut-off at the closing date.
entries.t: Your Books After a Stock Purchase: Recording the Deal Before the CPA Asks

entries.q: What is a funds flow statement in an acquisition?
entries.a: A document listing every payment made at closing, including payoffs, fees, payouts and loan proceeds, with the payer, payee and amount. It is the main source for recording the deal in the books.
entries.t: Your Books After a Stock Purchase: Recording the Deal Before the CPA Asks

entries.q: Who should record an acquisition in the books?
entries.a: An accountant experienced in acquisitions, ideally arranged before closing and given the closing documents as soon as the deal completes. The same person should prepare the working capital true-up, because the two depend on each other.
entries.t: Your Books After a Stock Purchase: Recording the Deal Before the CPA Asks

entries.q: What is return on invested capital for a location?
entries.a: The location's operating profit, after its share of shared costs, divided by the capital invested in it, including fit-out and equipment net of depreciation and the working capital it uses.
entries.t: ROIC, Not Revenue: Deciding Where the Next Dollar Goes Across Locations

entries.q: Why compare locations on return rather than revenue?
entries.a: Revenue shows size, not efficiency. Two locations with similar revenue can earn very different returns on the capital they use, and investment should go where each dollar earns the most.
entries.t: ROIC, Not Revenue: Deciding Where the Next Dollar Goes Across Locations

entries.q: When should a business slow investment in a location?
entries.a: When the location approaches the most it can sell. Close to that ceiling, each extra dollar invested earns less, and capital usually does better in locations with room to grow.
entries.t: ROIC, Not Revenue: Deciding Where the Next Dollar Goes Across Locations

entries.q: Are higher-cost markets better places to invest?
entries.a: Not automatically. Higher prices often come with higher rent, wages and investment costs. Compare return on invested capital before assuming a premium market earns more.
entries.t: ROIC, Not Revenue: Deciding Where the Next Dollar Goes Across Locations

entries.q: What is a working capital true-up?
entries.a: The calculation, after closing, of a business's actual net working capital on the closing date, compared with the target agreed in the purchase agreement. The purchase price is adjusted up or down for the difference.
entries.t: The 90-Day Working Capital True-Up: What It Involves and Why It Takes So Long

entries.q: How long does a working capital true-up take?
entries.a: Purchase agreements commonly allow around 90 days, but the work often takes longer than buyers expect, especially when the seller's books were kept on a cash basis without month-end cut-off.
entries.t: The 90-Day Working Capital True-Up: What It Involves and Why It Takes So Long

entries.q: How is a working capital true-up paid?
entries.a: Usually in cash, from an escrow, or by reducing the principal of a seller note. The purchase agreement should say which.
entries.t: The 90-Day Working Capital True-Up: What It Involves and Why It Takes So Long

entries.q: What happens if the buyer and seller disagree on the true-up?
entries.a: Most purchase agreements give the seller a period to review and dispute the calculation, and refer unresolved items to an independent accountant whose decision is binding.
entries.t: The 90-Day Working Capital True-Up: What It Involves and Why It Takes So Long

entries.q: What financial statements do buyers want when buying a business?
entries.a: Usually monthly profit and loss statements and balance sheets for three years plus the current year to date, business tax returns for three years, bank statements for the review period, receivables and payables ageing, revenue by customer, and a schedule of add-backs with evidence.
entries.t: Getting Your Financials Deal-Ready: What Buyers and Lenders Look For

entries.q: How far in advance should I prepare my financials for a sale?
entries.a: Ideally two years. Buyers value the trend over several years, and moving to accrual accounting, reconciling monthly and resolving compliance gaps takes months before the results show in the numbers.
entries.t: Getting Your Financials Deal-Ready: What Buyers and Lenders Look For

entries.q: What do lenders look for in a business acquisition?
entries.a: Whether historical earnings can cover the new debt. For SBA loans issued an SBA number from 1 October 2026, a first-time buyer needs at least 1.25x debt service coverage on historical or adjusted earnings, not projections.
entries.t: Getting Your Financials Deal-Ready: What Buyers and Lenders Look For

entries.q: Do I need a quality of earnings report to sell my business?
entries.a: Not always, but the buyer will usually commission one, and for SBA-financed deals of $3 million or more the lender must order one with a cash proof. A sell-side report helps you find and fix problems before buyers see them.
entries.t: Getting Your Financials Deal-Ready: What Buyers and Lenders Look For

entries.q: Should my books be on accrual or cash basis before a sale?
entries.a: Accrual. Buyers and lenders value businesses on accrual earnings, and a cash-basis file will be converted during diligence. Converting early lets you see and explain the effect before a buyer does.
entries.t: Getting Your Financials Deal-Ready: What Buyers and Lenders Look For

entries.q: What slows down due diligence the most?
entries.a: Unreconciled accounts, cash-basis books, personal spending mixed with business spending, add-backs without supporting evidence, revenue recorded in the wrong period, and unrecorded liabilities such as customer deposits or deferred revenue.
entries.t: Getting Your Financials Deal-Ready: What Buyers and Lenders Look For

entries.q: What is an add-back schedule?
entries.a: A list of adjustments to reported earnings, such as owner expenses or genuinely one-off costs, each with the amount, the reason it will not continue under a new owner, and the document that supports it.
entries.t: Getting Your Financials Deal-Ready: What Buyers and Lenders Look For

entries.q: How should a CAS firm handle client questions between monthly meetings?
entries.a: Separate routine questions about cash and recent changes, which can often be answered from the closed books, from judgement questions about decisions, which need the firm's time and should be scheduled or priced.
entries.t: The Questions Clients Ask Between Monthly Meetings, and Who Answers Them

entries.q: Should accounting firms charge for client questions?
entries.a: Many build an allowance into the engagement rather than billing each one. The aim is to price the judgement work properly without discouraging clients from asking questions they should ask.
entries.t: The Questions Clients Ask Between Monthly Meetings, and Who Answers Them

entries.q: How can a CAS practice serve more clients without more partners?
entries.a: By keeping senior time for judgement and moving routine answers to tools and team members, so the number of clients the firm can serve is no longer set by one person's hours.
entries.t: The Questions Clients Ask Between Monthly Meetings, and Who Answers Them

entries.q: What questions can clients answer from their own books?
entries.a: Usually cash position, who has not paid, what changed in revenue or expenses, and how the month compares with the last. Decisions about hiring, pricing or financing still need advice.
entries.t: The Questions Clients Ask Between Monthly Meetings, and Who Answers Them

entries.q: Should a growing company use an in-house bookkeeper or an outsourced one?
entries.a: It depends on size and the work involved. Many companies use both for a period, with an outside firm keeping the books and someone inside handling operational finance, until the split starts producing conflicting numbers or delays.
entries.t: An Outsourced Bookkeeper and an In-House One: When to Consolidate Into One Finance Team

entries.q: What are the signs bookkeeping should be consolidated?
entries.a: Two versions of the same number, a monthly close that waits on handoffs between parties, questions nobody clearly owns, and the owner acting as the person who reconciles the two.
entries.t: An Outsourced Bookkeeper and an In-House One: When to Consolidate Into One Finance Team

entries.q: What happens to the in-house bookkeeper when bookkeeping is outsourced?
entries.a: Often the operational part of the role continues, such as project tracking or client billing, while accounting moves to the outside team. Capture the person's knowledge and plan any change with them, not around them.
entries.t: An Outsourced Bookkeeper and an In-House One: When to Consolidate Into One Finance Team

entries.q: Is one outside finance team cheaper than two providers?
entries.a: Often, but cost should not be the main reason. Consolidation is worth doing when it fixes ownership, accuracy and timeliness of the numbers.
entries.t: An Outsourced Bookkeeper and an In-House One: When to Consolidate Into One Finance Team

entries.q: Can AI be used for due diligence on a small business acquisition?
entries.a: Yes, for reading contracts and ledgers at volume, flagging unusual items and comparing records. The findings still need to be checked against the source documents by someone who can judge what they mean.
entries.t: AI in Buy-Side Due Diligence: What It Can Check and What It Cannot

entries.q: What can AI not do in due diligence?
entries.a: It cannot make reliable judgements on add-backs or one-off items, see anything outside the data provided, or reliably detect errors designed to look normal. It can also give different answers to the same question.
entries.t: AI in Buy-Side Due Diligence: What It Can Check and What It Cannot

entries.q: Is it safe to upload data room files to ChatGPT or Claude?
entries.a: Only if the NDA allows it and the tool's data handling suits confidential material. Check where data is stored, whether it is used for training and who can access it, and ask the seller if unsure.
entries.t: AI in Buy-Side Due Diligence: What It Can Check and What It Cannot

entries.q: How do you make AI diligence findings reliable?
entries.a: Confirm every finding against its source document or ledger entry, record which checks were done by AI and which by a person, and ask the same question twice. A finding that changes is not yet a finding.
entries.t: AI in Buy-Side Due Diligence: What It Can Check and What It Cannot

entries.q: How should a hotel group allocate head-office costs to properties?
entries.a: Separate head-office costs first, then allocate each one on a basis that reflects what drives it, such as rooms available for revenue management or headcount for HR, and apply the methods consistently.
entries.t: Allocating Head-Office Costs Across a Multi-Property Hotel Group

entries.q: Should a hotel management company charge a management fee to its own properties?
entries.a: Many groups do, often a share of revenue with an incentive element, because it mirrors third-party management agreements and is familiar to lenders. Others allocate actual cost through intercompany entries. Both work if applied consistently.
entries.t: Allocating Head-Office Costs Across a Multi-Property Hotel Group

entries.q: Why do property results change after head-office allocation?
entries.a: Because shared costs such as finance, revenue management and the owner's time are added to each property. A property profitable before allocation can be loss-making after it, which means it is not covering its share of group overhead.
entries.t: Allocating Head-Office Costs Across a Multi-Property Hotel Group

entries.q: How do intercompany allocations affect consolidated results?
entries.a: They should net to zero. Charges from head office to each property are eliminated on consolidation, so the group total is unchanged while each property shows its full cost.
entries.t: Allocating Head-Office Costs Across a Multi-Property Hotel Group

entries.q: Can QuickBooks Online do project accounting?
entries.a: Yes, for many services firms. QuickBooks Online's Projects feature, on the Plus and Advanced plans, groups invoices, time, expenses and bills under each project so its profitability can be reported.
entries.t: Project Accounting in QuickBooks Online for Time-and-Materials Services Firms

entries.q: How do you record unbilled time in QuickBooks Online?
entries.a: At month end, recognise revenue for approved time worked but not yet invoiced, usually through an accrual entry against an unbilled receivables account, and reverse it when the invoice is raised.
entries.t: Project Accounting in QuickBooks Online for Time-and-Materials Services Firms

entries.q: How should a services firm account for a client retainer?
entries.a: As a liability when it is received. It becomes revenue as the work it covers is performed.
entries.t: Project Accounting in QuickBooks Online for Time-and-Materials Services Firms

entries.q: What is a project burn-down?
entries.a: A comparison of hours or cost used to date against the project budget, showing how much budget is left and whether the project is on track to finish within it.
entries.t: Project Accounting in QuickBooks Online for Time-and-Materials Services Firms

entries.q: Do I need separate project accounting software?
entries.a: Not always. Many time-and-materials firms run project accounting in QuickBooks Online with a separate timesheet tool. Firms with many concurrent fixed-fee projects often add project management or professional services software for budgets and resourcing.
entries.t: Project Accounting in QuickBooks Online for Time-and-Materials Services Firms

entries.q: What is customer concentration in an acquisition?
entries.a: Customer concentration is the share of a business's revenue or profit that comes from its largest customer or a small group of customers. High concentration means the loss of one relationship could materially reduce earnings and the value of the business.
entries.t: Customer Concentration in an Acquisition: How Lenders Read It and How Deals Get Structured

entries.q: How do lenders view customer concentration?
entries.a: They test whether the business could still service its debt if the largest customer left. Any customer whose loss would push debt service coverage below the lender's threshold will draw close attention from the credit committee.
entries.t: Customer Concentration in an Acquisition: How Lenders Read It and How Deals Get Structured

entries.q: How can a buyer protect against customer concentration?
entries.a: Common structures include a seller note that is reduced if revenue falls below a set level after closing, a standby note tied to the customer being retained, and a larger equity contribution to leave room in debt service coverage.
entries.t: Customer Concentration in an Acquisition: How Lenders Read It and How Deals Get Structured

entries.q: Should concentration be measured on revenue or profit?
entries.a: Both. Revenue share is the usual headline, but gross profit share shows what the loss of a customer would do to cash available for debt service, which is what lenders care about.
entries.t: Customer Concentration in an Acquisition: How Lenders Read It and How Deals Get Structured

entries.q: Which countries have e-invoicing mandates in effect in 2026?
entries.a: As of 21 October 2026, mandates are in effect in Belgium, Croatia for VAT-registered taxpayers, Poland and France for receiving and for large and mid-sized issuers. Germany has required businesses to receive e-invoices since 1 January 2025, and India's 30-day reporting limit and Mexico's CFDI 4.0 also apply.
entries.t: E-Invoicing Mandates 2026–2028: A Timeline for Multi-Country Finance Teams

entries.q: When does e-invoicing become mandatory for all businesses in Germany?
entries.a: From 1 January 2028. Invoices other than e-invoices are allowed for 2025 and 2026 supplies until 31 December 2026, and for 2027 supplies only where prior-year turnover was not more than €800,000 or the invoice is exchanged by EDI.
entries.t: E-Invoicing Mandates 2026–2028: A Timeline for Multi-Country Finance Teams

entries.q: When do French SMEs have to issue e-invoices?
entries.a: From 1 September 2027. Since 1 September 2026 all French businesses must be able to receive e-invoices, and large and mid-sized companies must issue them.
entries.t: E-Invoicing Mandates 2026–2028: A Timeline for Multi-Country Finance Teams

entries.q: Is Spain's VERI*FACTU an e-invoicing mandate?
entries.a: No, VERI*FACTU sets rules for billing software rather than for exchanging B2B e-invoices. Companies must adapt before 1 January 2027 and other taxpayers before 1 July 2027, subject to further change.
entries.t: E-Invoicing Mandates 2026–2028: A Timeline for Multi-Country Finance Teams

entries.q: What is India's 30-day e-invoice reporting rule?
entries.a: Since 1 April 2025, taxpayers with aggregate annual turnover of ₹10 crore and above cannot report e-invoices, credit notes or debit notes older than 30 days on the invoice registration portal.
entries.t: E-Invoicing Mandates 2026–2028: A Timeline for Multi-Country Finance Teams

entries.q: How should an HVAC company record maintenance agreements?
entries.a: As revenue earned over the term of the agreement. An annual agreement paid upfront is recorded as a liability when paid and recognised month by month as the service period passes.
entries.t: Bookkeeping for HVAC Companies: The Numbers an Owner in the Field Needs

entries.q: What is job costing for HVAC?
entries.a: Tracking the materials, labor and other direct costs of each job against its revenue, so the gross margin of every install and service call can be seen when it is completed.
entries.t: Bookkeeping for HVAC Companies: The Numbers an Owner in the Field Needs

entries.q: Should HVAC parts on trucks be counted as inventory?
entries.a: Yes. Parts held on trucks are inventory until used on a job. Expensing them when bought understates the assets of the business and distorts the cost of each month.
entries.t: Bookkeeping for HVAC Companies: The Numbers an Owner in the Field Needs

entries.q: What financial reports does an HVAC owner need?
entries.a: A short weekly view: cash today and for the coming weeks, unpaid invoices by age, gross margin on completed jobs, and booked work ahead. Full monthly statements support it.
entries.t: Bookkeeping for HVAC Companies: The Numbers an Owner in the Field Needs

entries.q: What does an accounting health check look at?
entries.a: It reviews an accounting file against published standards, checking reconciliation, revenue recognition, payroll and contractor obligations, period controls, coding consistency and the monthly close rhythm, and scores the results by area.
entries.t: What an Accounting Health Check Looks At, and What a Low Score Means

entries.q: Is an accounting health check the same as an audit?
entries.a: No. A health check is an automated diagnostic. It does not give assurance on the financial statements and does not replace an audit, review or compilation by a licensed CPA.
entries.t: What an Accounting Health Check Looks At, and What a Low Score Means

entries.q: Does running a health check change my QuickBooks file?
entries.a: Not with a read-only connection. Navigator's health check connects through Intuit's standard consent screen with read-only accounting scope, so nothing is created, changed or deleted.
entries.t: What an Accounting Health Check Looks At, and What a Low Score Means

entries.q: What does a low decision readiness score mean?
entries.a: That the books are not yet set up to answer business questions on time, usually because there is no fixed close date, no regular review or no budget to compare against. The entries themselves may still be accurate.
entries.t: What an Accounting Health Check Looks At, and What a Low Score Means

entries.q: How long does an accounting health check take?
entries.a: A few minutes for the automated checks, plus about a minute for six questions on how the close and review work. Larger files take longer to read.
entries.t: What an Accounting Health Check Looks At, and What a Low Score Means

entries.q: Can a seller note count toward the SBA equity injection?
entries.a: Yes, partly. Under SOP 50 10 8.1 a seller note on full standby can make up part of the required injection, but at least half of the injection must be the buyer's own unborrowed cash.
entries.t: Seller Financing Under SBA SOP 50 10 8.1: Standby Notes, Forgivable Notes and Earnouts

entries.q: How long must an SBA seller standby note stay on standby?
entries.a: Under SOP 50 10 8.1, a seller note on full standby must sit for 36 months before it can be refinanced, up from 24 months under the previous version.
entries.t: Seller Financing Under SBA SOP 50 10 8.1: Standby Notes, Forgivable Notes and Earnouts

entries.q: Are earnouts allowed in an SBA acquisition?
entries.a: No. SBA rules require a fixed purchase price in a change-of-ownership loan, so a payment that depends on the business's future results is not permitted.
entries.t: Seller Financing Under SBA SOP 50 10 8.1: Standby Notes, Forgivable Notes and Earnouts

entries.q: What is a forgivable seller note?
entries.a: A seller note that can be reduced if a defined measure, usually tied to historical results such as revenue from named contracts, falls short after closing. It is often used in SBA deals in place of an earnout.
entries.t: Seller Financing Under SBA SOP 50 10 8.1: Standby Notes, Forgivable Notes and Earnouts

entries.q: Does a seller note affect debt service coverage?
entries.a: A note paid alongside the SBA loan counts against coverage from the first payment. A note on full standby does not while it is on standby, but it will once payments begin.
entries.t: Seller Financing Under SBA SOP 50 10 8.1: Standby Notes, Forgivable Notes and Earnouts

entries.q: What should I look for when buying an accounting firm?
entries.a: Revenue by client and by managing partner, staff tenure and capacity, realization against standard rates, the value of work in progress, and the month-by-month cash cycle across tax season. Retention of clients and staff decides most outcomes.
entries.t: Buying an Accounting Firm: The Finance Diligence That Decides the Deal

entries.q: Can someone who is not a CPA buy an accounting firm?
entries.a: Often yes for bookkeeping, tax preparation and advisory work. For firms that perform attest work such as audits and reviews, state rules usually require a majority of owners to hold a CPA licence, so a non-CPA buyer may need a licensed partner or a different structure.
entries.t: Buying an Accounting Firm: The Finance Diligence That Decides the Deal

entries.q: How do accounting firm acquisitions usually lose value?
entries.a: Most often through clients who follow the selling partner rather than staying with the firm, and through staff who leave during the first busy season under new ownership.
entries.t: Buying an Accounting Firm: The Finance Diligence That Decides the Deal

entries.q: How do I handle the first tax season after buying a practice?
entries.a: Plan delivery capacity before closing, because the team will be absorbing a change of ownership while working at its busiest. Firms often add temporary or partner capacity so the existing team is not stretched past what it can carry.
entries.t: Buying an Accounting Firm: The Finance Diligence That Decides the Deal

entries.q: What is billable utilization?
entries.a: Billable utilization is the share of paid working hours that were billed to clients. It is calculated as billable hours divided by available hours, where available hours are paid hours less holidays and paid leave.
entries.t: Utilization Rate for Professional Services Firms: How to Measure It From QuickBooks and Gusto

entries.q: How do you calculate utilization rate from QuickBooks and Gusto?
entries.a: Take paid hours by person from Gusto, remove holidays and paid leave, and take billable hours from your timesheet tool, checked against what QuickBooks shows as invoiced. Divide billable by available for each person, then roll up by team.
entries.t: Utilization Rate for Professional Services Firms: How to Measure It From QuickBooks and Gusto

entries.q: What is the difference between utilization and realized rate?
entries.a: Utilization measures how much of the paid time was billed. Realized rate measures the revenue earned per billable hour. A firm needs both, because high utilization at a low rate can still produce poor margins.
entries.t: Utilization Rate for Professional Services Firms: How to Measure It From QuickBooks and Gusto

entries.q: Should non-billable staff be included in utilization?
entries.a: Report them separately. Including leaders, sales and operations staff in the same average makes the delivery team's utilization look lower than it is and hides where the real gap sits.
entries.t: Utilization Rate for Professional Services Firms: How to Measure It From QuickBooks and Gusto

entries.q: What is a working capital peg?
entries.a: A working capital peg is the level of net working capital the buyer and seller agree a business needs to operate normally. The seller delivers that amount at closing, and the purchase price is adjusted up or down for any difference.
entries.t: The Working Capital Peg: How Buyers and Sellers Agree What Normal Looks Like

entries.q: How is a working capital peg calculated?
entries.a: Usually as an average of monthly net working capital over a recent period, often the trailing twelve months, adjusted for seasonality and for items both parties agree to exclude, such as old receivables or related-party balances.
entries.t: The Working Capital Peg: How Buyers and Sellers Agree What Normal Looks Like

entries.q: What is excluded from net working capital in an acquisition?
entries.a: Cash and debt are normally excluded because they are handled separately in the price. Many deals also exclude receivables past a set age, obsolete inventory and balances with the owner or related parties.
entries.t: The Working Capital Peg: How Buyers and Sellers Agree What Normal Looks Like

entries.q: What happens if working capital at closing is below the peg?
entries.a: The purchase price is reduced by the shortfall. The adjustment is usually settled in the post-closing true-up, often against a seller note or an escrow.
entries.t: The Working Capital Peg: How Buyers and Sellers Agree What Normal Looks Like

entries.q: Should the peg use a 12-month average?
entries.a: Not always. Seasonal businesses should reflect the month of closing, and fast-growing ones need a shorter or adjusted period. If receivables are rising faster than revenue during diligence, a longer average will understate what the business needs.
entries.t: The Working Capital Peg: How Buyers and Sellers Agree What Normal Looks Like

entries.q: Is it safe to outsource accounting to India?
entries.a: It can be, if the work stays in your own systems under logins you control, the partner's infrastructure is certified to a recognised standard such as SOC 2 or ISO/IEC 27001, and access is reviewed and removed promptly when people leave. Ask to see the evidence rather than relying on the sales deck.
entries.t: Outsourced Accounting in India for US Companies: What to Check Before You Sign

entries.q: How much does outsourced accounting in India cost?
entries.a: Less than a US-only team for the same scope, because execution is priced at Indian salaries. Compare quotes on scope rather than hours. A low hourly rate means little if the work has to be checked again by someone in the US.
entries.t: Outsourced Accounting in India for US Companies: What to Check Before You Sign

entries.q: Can an Indian accounting firm file my US taxes?
entries.a: US tax returns should be signed by a licensed US preparer, usually a CPA or enrolled agent. An India-based partner can prepare the books and the schedules your US preparer files from, which is how most well-run arrangements work.
entries.t: Outsourced Accounting in India for US Companies: What to Check Before You Sign

entries.q: What is hybridshore accounting?
entries.a: A delivery model that splits finance work by the kind of work rather than by location. Review, judgement and accountability stay with US-based finance leadership in your time zone, and execution sits with an employed team in India working in your systems.
entries.t: Outsourced Accounting in India for US Companies: What to Check Before You Sign

entries.q: What should I ask an offshore accounting firm before signing?
entries.a: Who the named people on your account are and whether they are employees, who reviews the work and where, what the close calendar is, whether they work in your system, what happens to your data if you leave, and which work your CPA will still do.
entries.t: Outsourced Accounting in India for US Companies: What to Check Before You Sign

entries.q: What is a proof of cash?
entries.a: A proof of cash reconciles cash receipts and payments recorded in the accounting system to deposits and withdrawals on the bank statements, month by month, for the whole review period. It shows whether the books describe money that actually moved through the bank.
entries.t: Proof of Cash in a Quality of Earnings: What SBA Lenders Now Require

entries.q: When does an SBA loan require a quality of earnings with a cash proof?
entries.a: Under SOP 50 10 8.1, for loans issued an SBA loan number on or after 1 October 2026, a business acquisition with a purchase price of $3 million or more requires a lender-ordered quality of earnings report that includes a cash proof.
entries.t: Proof of Cash in a Quality of Earnings: What SBA Lenders Now Require

entries.q: Is a proof of cash the same as a bank reconciliation?
entries.a: No. A bank reconciliation agrees the closing balance at month end. A proof of cash also agrees the total receipts and payments for the month, so it catches errors that offset each other and leave the closing balance looking correct.
entries.t: Proof of Cash in a Quality of Earnings: What SBA Lenders Now Require

entries.q: How many months does a proof of cash cover?
entries.a: It covers the same period as the quality of earnings review, which the reviewer sets, with every month in it reconciled.
entries.t: Proof of Cash in a Quality of Earnings: What SBA Lenders Now Require

entries.q: Can a seller prepare for a proof of cash in advance?
entries.a: Yes. Reconcile every account monthly, separate owner transactions from business ones, convert the review period to accrual if the books are kept on cash, and document every add-back against a bank payment.
entries.t: Proof of Cash in a Quality of Earnings: What SBA Lenders Now Require

entries.q: Can a green card holder get an SBA loan in 2026?
entries.a: No. Since 1 March 2026, the SBA 7(a) and 504 programs require every owner of the borrowing business to be a US citizen or US national with a principal residence in the United States. Lawful permanent residents do not meet that test.
entries.t: Buying a Business as a Green Card Holder in 2026: Financing Without SBA

entries.q: Does the rule apply if the green card holder owns only a small stake?
entries.a: Yes. The SBA's notice covers businesses owned in whole or in part by a foreign national, and the earlier allowance for small foreign stakes was rescinded. Any ownership by a permanent resident makes the application ineligible.
entries.t: Buying a Business as a Green Card Holder in 2026: Financing Without SBA

entries.q: Which SBA programs does the restriction cover?
entries.a: The 7(a) and 504 loan programs from 1 March 2026. On 9 March 2026 the SBA announced a further notice extending it to the Microloan and Surety Bond programs.
entries.t: Buying a Business as a Green Card Holder in 2026: Financing Without SBA

entries.q: How are green card holders financing acquisitions now?
entries.a: Mostly through a mix of seller financing, conventional bank loans, private credit and investor equity. Each asks for more equity or more seller paper than an SBA loan did, and each looks more closely at earnings quality and monthly reporting.
entries.t: Buying a Business as a Green Card Holder in 2026: Financing Without SBA

entries.q: Can a seller earnout be used without SBA financing?
entries.a: Yes, in most cases. SBA rules do not allow earnouts in a change-of-ownership loan, but conventional and private lenders often accept one if it can be paid from operating cash flow without breaching a covenant.
entries.t: Buying a Business as a Green Card Holder in 2026: Financing Without SBA

entries.q: How long does it take a US company to incorporate in India?
entries.a: Usually a few weeks once the apostilled documents are ready. A first payroll run takes longer, because the bank account, capital receipt, share allotment, GST and state registrations all follow incorporation.
entries.t: Setting Up a Subsidiary in India as a US Company: What It Actually Takes

entries.q: Does an Indian subsidiary need a resident director?
entries.a: Yes. At least one director must stay in India for 182 days or more in the financial year, under Section 149(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, with a proportionate test in the first year.
entries.t: Setting Up a Subsidiary in India as a US Company: What It Actually Takes

entries.q: Is there a minimum capital requirement for an Indian private limited company?
entries.a: No. There is no statutory minimum paid-up capital, though the capital should cover working capital until the first intercompany payments arrive.
entries.t: Setting Up a Subsidiary in India as a US Company: What It Actually Takes

entries.q: Does the US parent file Form 5471 for its Indian subsidiary?
entries.a: Yes, if the subsidiary is treated as a corporation for US tax, which is the default for an Indian private limited company. If the parent elects disregarded treatment on Form 8832, it files Form 8858 instead.
entries.t: Setting Up a Subsidiary in India as a US Company: What It Actually Takes

entries.q: Does the Indian subsidiary charge GST to its US parent?
entries.a: Usually not. Services supplied to a parent outside India and paid for in foreign currency normally qualify as zero-rated exports, and the subsidiary files a Letter of Undertaking so it can export without paying IGST upfront.
entries.t: Setting Up a Subsidiary in India as a US Company: What It Actually Takes

entries.q: What transfer pricing mark-up should an Indian subsidiary charge its US parent?
entries.a: It depends on what the subsidiary does and which risks it bears. For IT and IT-enabled services, India's safe harbour from tax year 2026-27 is a 15.5% mark-up on operating costs, and the same mark-up has to be defensible under US Section 482.
entries.t: Setting Up a Subsidiary in India as a US Company: What It Actually Takes

entries.q: Does a subsidiary remove permanent establishment risk for the US parent?
entries.a: Not entirely. Risk returns if subsidiary staff conclude contracts for the parent, or if US employees perform services in India for the subsidiary, which under the India-US treaty can create a service PE without the usual 90-day threshold.
entries.t: Setting Up a Subsidiary in India as a US Company: What It Actually Takes

entries.q: How do you measure AI ROI in finance?
entries.a: Measure hours per unit, error and rework rates, cycle time and cash effects for each process against a baseline taken before the change, then set the money value of those changes against the full cost, including the time people spend reviewing AI output.
entries.t: Measuring AI ROI in Finance: Hours, Errors, Cycle Time and Cash

entries.q: What share of finance teams see a return from AI?
entries.a: Survey answers vary with the question asked. In Gartner's June 2026 release, only 7% of finance organizations reported a high or very high impact, while KPMG's May 2026 survey found 71% of senior finance leaders saying AI was meeting or exceeding ROI expectations.
entries.t: Measuring AI ROI in Finance: Hours, Errors, Cycle Time and Cash

entries.q: Do hours saved by AI count as return?
entries.a: Only when they are redeployed to named work or avoid hiring that would otherwise have happened. Hours that are absorbed into the existing week are capacity, and should be reported as such.
entries.t: Measuring AI ROI in Finance: Hours, Errors, Cycle Time and Cash

entries.q: Which costs belong in a finance AI business case?
entries.a: Licences, build and integration, data preparation, controls and audit work, ongoing accuracy monitoring, model changes, and the time people spend checking AI output.
entries.t: Measuring AI ROI in Finance: Hours, Errors, Cycle Time and Cash

entries.q: How do you separate AI's impact from process improvements?
entries.a: Label process fixes made during the project separately, and where possible compare an entity or unit that adopted the change with one that did not over the same period.
entries.t: Measuring AI ROI in Finance: Hours, Errors, Cycle Time and Cash

entries.q: What is an AI proof of concept in finance?
entries.a: It is a time-limited test of whether an AI-assisted version of one finance process performs better than the current one, on the company's own data, against a baseline and success criteria agreed in advance.
entries.t: AI Proof of Concept in Finance: Designing a Pilot That Reaches Production

entries.q: How long should a finance AI pilot run?
entries.a: About ten to twelve weeks from scoping to decision is a workable shape for a single process. The decision date should be fixed on the first day, with at most one extension for a specific reason.
entries.t: AI Proof of Concept in Finance: Designing a Pilot That Reaches Production

entries.q: Why do AI pilots in finance fail to reach production?
entries.a: Usually because there was no baseline, success was defined after the fact, nobody owned the control, write access triggered a late security review, or there was no date on which a decision had to be made.
entries.t: AI Proof of Concept in Finance: Designing a Pilot That Reaches Production

entries.q: What success criteria should a finance AI pilot have?
entries.a: Numeric thresholds for hours per unit, output accuracy on a reviewed sample, rework or exception rate and cycle time, set before the pilot starts, plus a stop criterion and the control evidence the auditors will need.
entries.t: AI Proof of Concept in Finance: Designing a Pilot That Reaches Production

entries.q: Should an AI pilot have write access to the ERP?
entries.a: No, not at the pilot stage. Read-only access with a person posting or releasing anything keeps the ERP as the book of record and avoids a security review that can outlast the pilot.
entries.t: AI Proof of Concept in Finance: Designing a Pilot That Reaches Production

entries.q: Should we test our ERP vendor's AI features or build our own?
entries.a: Test what the vendor already offers first, and compare it with a custom build on the same baseline if the gap matters. Vendor descriptions of AI features are not evidence of how they perform on your data.
entries.t: AI Proof of Concept in Finance: Designing a Pilot That Reaches Production

entries.q: What is AI variance analysis?
entries.a: AI variance analysis uses software to calculate movements against budget, forecast or prior periods, identify the transactions behind them and draft plain-language commentary for a finance professional to review and approve.
entries.t: AI Variance Analysis: Commentary a Board Can Trust

entries.q: Can AI write board variance commentary?
entries.a: AI can write a good first draft, provided the figures come from the ledger and a named reviewer confirms each explanation before the commentary goes to the board. It should not be the final author.
entries.t: AI Variance Analysis: Commentary a Board Can Trust

entries.q: How do you stop AI from inventing explanations?
entries.a: Require evidence for every explanation, such as journal entries, operational data or a confirmation from the budget owner, and treat any cause inferred only from an account name or past pattern as a question rather than a finding.
entries.t: AI Variance Analysis: Commentary a Board Can Trust

entries.q: What materiality threshold should variance commentary use?
entries.a: Use a threshold that combines a percentage and an amount, agreed before the period starts and documented, so that commentary focuses on movements that matter and small lines with large percentage swings do not crowd them out.
entries.t: AI Variance Analysis: Commentary a Board Can Trust

entries.q: Who should review AI-generated variance commentary?
entries.a: A named finance professional who understands the business, usually the FP&A lead or controller, with the CFO accountable for anything that goes to the board. The review should be recorded.
entries.t: AI Variance Analysis: Commentary a Board Can Trust

entries.q: How is AI used in the month-end close?
entries.a: AI is used mainly to match transactions in reconciliations, calculate and explain movements in flux analysis, and draft first-version commentary. People review the exceptions, the causes and anything that leaves the finance team.
entries.t: AI in the Month-End Close: Reconciliations, Flux Analysis and Commentary

entries.q: Can AI do account reconciliations?
entries.a: AI can reliably do the matching part, sorting items into matched, potentially matched and unmatched. Potential matches, unmatched items and proposed adjustments still need a preparer and a reviewer.
entries.t: AI in the Month-End Close: Reconciliations, Flux Analysis and Commentary

entries.q: What is flux analysis, and can AI do it?
entries.a: Flux analysis compares balances with a prior period or budget and explains material movements. AI can calculate the movements and gather the transactions behind them, but someone who knows the business must confirm the cause.
entries.t: AI in the Month-End Close: Reconciliations, Flux Analysis and Commentary

entries.q: Does AI-written close commentary need review?
entries.a: Yes. Figures should come from the ledger and tie to the trial balance, and a named reviewer should check causes, emphasis and omissions before the commentary is used.
entries.t: AI in the Month-End Close: Reconciliations, Flux Analysis and Commentary

entries.q: How long should a month-end close take?
entries.a: About six calendar days is typical: APQC's cross-industry median from trial balance to agreed consolidation is 6 days, against 5 for top performers and 10 for bottom performers (2022 data, published 2025).
entries.t: AI in the Month-End Close: Reconciliations, Flux Analysis and Commentary

entries.q: What does finance support cost after an SBA acquisition?
entries.a: For most acquired businesses under $10M in revenue, a full-stack outsourced function runs $1,500–$5,000 per month, covering the close, lender reporting, forecasting and covenant tracking. Compare that against roughly $213,000 fully loaded for an in-house finance manager, or $65,000 for a bookkeeper who will not cover the covenant work at all. Against other providers rather than against hiring, CFOLogic's Hybridshore model delivers the same scope 30–50% below what most firms charge, because senior judgment and execution capacity are priced separately rather than both at US headcount rates.
entries.t: Outsourced Accounting for SBA Acquisitions: Cost, Scope and Covenant Reporting

entries.q: What changes under SOP 50 10 8.1 on 1 October 2026?
entries.a: For a first-time buyer, the debt service coverage floor rises from 1.15x to 1.25x and must be met on historical or adjusted earnings rather than projections. Purchase prices of $3 million or more trigger a lender-ordered Quality of Earnings report with a cash proof. At least half the equity injection must be your own unborrowed cash, and seller notes on standby must sit 36 months before refinancing. The rules apply by SBA loan number date, not application date.
entries.t: Outsourced Accounting for SBA Acquisitions: Cost, Scope and Covenant Reporting

entries.q: Do I need a CFO after buying a business with an SBA loan?
entries.a: Usually not a full-time one, and not immediately. What the note requires is a reliable close, defensible covenant reporting and a forward cash view. That is controller and FP&A work with senior review over it. A full-time CFO becomes the right answer later, at which point the execution team stays and works to them.
entries.t: Outsourced Accounting for SBA Acquisitions: Cost, Scope and Covenant Reporting

entries.q: How soon should the finance function be in place?
entries.a: Before close if possible, in month one otherwise. The opening balance sheet has to be set correctly at close, and reconstructing it six months later is expensive. Cleanup on the seller's books should be scoped during diligence, while you still have leverage and the seller is still reachable.
entries.t: Outsourced Accounting for SBA Acquisitions: Cost, Scope and Covenant Reporting

entries.q: Will an outsourced team work if the seller's books are a mess?
entries.a: That is the common case rather than the exception. Cleanup is scoped and priced as a separate project, assessed first so you know what you are inheriting. The ongoing monthly engagement assumes current books, which is why the two are quoted separately.
entries.t: Outsourced Accounting for SBA Acquisitions: Cost, Scope and Covenant Reporting

entries.q: Does Dynamics 365 Finance have AI for collections?
entries.a: Yes. Summary by Copilot produces an AI-generated summary of a customer's overdue invoices, payment history and remaining credit, and an AI-generated draft of a reminder email, according to Microsoft Learn documentation updated in September 2026.
entries.t: AI in Order-to-Cash on Microsoft Dynamics 365: Where to Start

entries.q: What does the account reconciliation agent in Dynamics 365 Finance do?
entries.a: It helps reconcile the general ledger with the accounts payable, accounts receivable, tax and bank subledgers. With the Copilot-powered agent switched on, each difference gets a proposed action, an analysis and a justification for a person to review.
entries.t: AI in Order-to-Cash on Microsoft Dynamics 365: Where to Start

entries.q: Where should a CFO start with AI in order-to-cash?
entries.a: Start by testing the AI features you already license, then pick one exception queue, such as disputes or unapplied cash, and build a read-only cross-customer view with owners and aging for that queue before widening.
entries.t: AI in Order-to-Cash on Microsoft Dynamics 365: Where to Start

entries.q: Do we need a separate tool on top of Dynamics 365?
entries.a: Not always. If per-customer summaries and the reconciliation agent cover your needs, start there; a layer adds value when you need one view of exceptions across all customers, with an owner and an age on each, and data from outside Dynamics.
entries.t: AI in Order-to-Cash on Microsoft Dynamics 365: Where to Start

entries.q: Can AI send collection emails automatically?
entries.a: It can, but it should not at the start. Have AI draft the email, and have a collector review and send it, so that tone, accuracy and any open dispute are checked by someone accountable for the customer relationship.
entries.t: AI in Order-to-Cash on Microsoft Dynamics 365: Where to Start

entries.q: What can AI do in accounts payable today?
entries.a: Today AI can reliably classify invoices and exceptions, suggest matches, route exceptions to owners and flag anomalies in the payment proposal, all as suggestions a person reviews.
entries.t: AI in Accounts Payable on SAP: What Works and What Still Needs People

entries.q: Can AI approve invoices in SAP?
entries.a: It should not approve them. Approval is delegated authority that belongs to a named person, so AI should prepare the evidence and a person should approve.
entries.t: AI in Accounts Payable on SAP: What Works and What Still Needs People

entries.q: Should an AI tool write back to SAP?
entries.a: Not in a first project. A read-only tool is quicker to test and cannot make a wrong posting; write access can follow once controls, logging and ownership are in place.
entries.t: AI in Accounts Payable on SAP: What Works and What Still Needs People

entries.q: How many companies use AI in accounts payable?
entries.a: Published surveys suggest AP is one of the commonest uses. Gartner's 2025 survey put AP process automation at 37% among top AI use cases, and Hackett's 2026 study, sample not disclosed, reported 33% of organizations scaling AI in AP.
entries.t: AI in Accounts Payable on SAP: What Works and What Still Needs People

entries.q: What does it cost to process an invoice?
entries.a: APQC's cross-industry median total cost to process AP is $6.50 per invoice, across 6,546 companies. Ardent Partners' vendor research reports an average of $9.84, measured differently.
entries.t: AI in Accounts Payable on SAP: What Works and What Still Needs People

entries.q: What changes in internal controls when AI is used in financial reporting?
entries.a: The control around an AI-assisted step has to cover the AI's output: what the reviewer checks and against what source, whether AI-produced information is complete and accurate, how changes to prompts and models are controlled, and what evidence is kept. The basic principles of control design stay the same.
entries.t: AI Internal Controls: What Changes When AI Touches Financial Reporting

entries.q: Is the AI or the reviewer the control?
entries.a: In most AI-assisted steps the human review is the control, and the AI output is an input to it. Write the control description so the reviewer is clearly accountable and the review is specific about what is checked.
entries.t: AI Internal Controls: What Changes When AI Touches Financial Reporting

entries.q: How should prompts and AI models be handled under change management?
entries.a: Treat prompts, instructions, source libraries and access settings as configuration: changes are requested, tested against a fixed set of cases, approved by someone other than the person who made them, and recorded. Ask vendors how model updates are announced and whether a version can be pinned.
entries.t: AI Internal Controls: What Changes When AI Touches Financial Reporting

entries.q: Can an AI agent create a segregation of duties conflict?
entries.a: Yes, an AI agent with rights to both create and approve a transaction, or to change vendor bank details and propose payments, is a conflict just as it would be for a person. Give each agent its own account and include it in the SoD matrix and access reviews.
entries.t: AI Internal Controls: What Changes When AI Touches Financial Reporting

entries.q: What will auditors ask about AI in financial reporting?
entries.a: Expect questions about where AI is used and in what role, the related controls, the completeness and accuracy of AI-produced information, change management for prompts and models, system access, and retained evidence. Discuss these with your auditors before year-end.
entries.t: AI Internal Controls: What Changes When AI Touches Financial Reporting

entries.q: Are most finance teams ready for audit of AI-enabled processes?
entries.a: Fewer than half say they are: in KPMG's May 2026 survey, 42% of organizations were fully assurance-ready for AI-enabled finance processes. The rest have work to do on controls, evidence or both before relying on AI in reporting.
entries.t: AI Internal Controls: What Changes When AI Touches Financial Reporting

entries.q: What does a quality of earnings report cover?
entries.a: A quality of earnings report analyzes whether reported earnings are sustainable and repeatable. It assesses the seller's proposed add-backs, identifies adjustments the seller has not made, sets out the net working capital position and recommends a peg, and lists items a buyer would expect to fund, assume or deduct from the equity price. It is not an audit and expresses no assurance on the financial statements.
entries.t: What a Buy-Side Quality of Earnings Actually Finds

entries.q: Why is adjusted EBITDA usually lower than the seller's number?
entries.a: Because a seller's presentation is built from what should be added back, and a buyer needs what should be taken out as well. In this example the seller's own add-backs were mostly sound. The gap came from costs the business does not currently bear but will after close, income that is not trading performance, and accounting errors that flattered the result.
entries.t: What a Buy-Side Quality of Earnings Actually Finds

entries.q: What are debt-like items?
entries.a: Obligations a buyer will have to fund or assume that do not appear as debt on the balance sheet. In this example they included unrecorded accrued paid time off, an under-collected lodging tax exposure with penalties, equipment finance leases, franchise transfer fees triggered by the change of control, brand-mandated improvement plans, and the above-market element of a related-party ground lease.
entries.t: What a Buy-Side Quality of Earnings Actually Finds

entries.q: Is a quality of earnings worth it on a smaller deal?
entries.a: The findings above scale down. On a $3M to $10M transaction the same three patterns — uncompensated owner functions, committed capital absent from the price, and a favorable working capital peg — routinely account for more than the cost of the work.
entries.t: What a Buy-Side Quality of Earnings Actually Finds

entries.q: What does a fractional CFO cost?
entries.a: Market benchmarks put the median rate at $175 an hour, with most engagements between $125 and $220 (Go Fractional, 2026).
