At ten hours a week that works out to roughly $63,000 to $110,000 a year, against a full-time CFO base salary range of $195,500 to $321,750 (Robert Half, 2026). The fractional rate covers the CFO's time only, not accounting or analyst capacity.
entries.t: Fractional CFO Services: Cost and When You Need One

entries.q: What is the difference between a fractional CFO and an interim CFO?
entries.a: Fractional is a permanent arrangement at part-time hours. Interim is a full-time seat filled for a fixed period, usually after a departure or during a transaction. Interim engagements are shorter and cost considerably more per month.
entries.t: Fractional CFO Services: Cost and When You Need One

entries.q: At what revenue should a company hire a fractional CFO?
entries.a: There is no reliable revenue threshold. Most companies find the role earns its cost somewhere between $3M and $10M, but the trigger is an event — a raise, a covenant, a margin problem, an acquisition — rather than a number on the top line.
entries.t: Fractional CFO Services: Cost and When You Need One

entries.q: Can a fractional CFO replace an accountant or bookkeeper?
entries.a: No. They sit above that work and depend on it. A fractional CFO working from an unreliable ledger will spend the engagement fixing accounting at CFO rates, which is the most expensive way to buy bookkeeping.
entries.t: Fractional CFO Services: Cost and When You Need One

entries.q: How long does a fractional CFO engagement last?
entries.a: Commonly twelve to thirty-six months. Shorter than that usually means the scope was a project. Longer usually means the arrangement has become the permanent finance function, which is fine as long as everyone has said so out loud.
entries.t: Fractional CFO Services: Cost and When You Need One

entries.q: Is a fractional CFO worth it for a small business?
entries.a: It depends on whether your problems are decisions or data. If you cannot get accurate numbers, buy accounting capacity first. If you have accurate numbers and cannot decide what to do with them, that is what a CFO is for.
entries.t: Fractional CFO Services: Cost and When You Need One

entries.q: What is an AI use policy for finance?
entries.a: An AI use policy for finance is a short written set of rules covering which AI tools the finance team may use, with which data, for which tasks, what review is required, and what records are kept. It usually sits as an annex to, or alongside, the company's general AI policy.
entries.t: An AI Use Policy for the Finance Function: What to Put in It

entries.q: What should an AI use policy include?
entries.a: It should include scope, roles, approved tools, data classes, permitted and prohibited uses, review requirements, record keeping, incident handling, training and a process for exceptions and updates. The tool list and data class table work best as appendices that change more often than the policy.
entries.t: An AI Use Policy for the Finance Function: What to Put in It

entries.q: Does the EU AI Act apply to finance teams using AI?
entries.a: It can, depending on where the company operates and how AI is used, so check scope with counsel. The AI literacy obligation has applied since 2 February 2025. After the Digital Omnibus, high-risk obligations apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and from 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems.
entries.t: An AI Use Policy for the Finance Function: What to Put in It

entries.q: Do we need ISO/IEC 42001 certification?
entries.a: Most finance functions do not need certification, though the standard is a useful reference for how to structure AI policy, roles, risk assessment and review. Certification is a company-level decision, usually driven by customers or regulators.
entries.t: An AI Use Policy for the Finance Function: What to Put in It

entries.q: Who should own the AI use policy in finance?
entries.a: The CFO should own the finance AI use policy, with IT security, legal and the controller contributing to the sections they know best. The tool list and data class table each need a named owner who keeps them current.
entries.t: An AI Use Policy for the Finance Function: What to Put in It

entries.q: How often should an AI use policy be reviewed?
entries.a: Review it twice a year while tools are changing quickly, and sooner when a new tool is approved, an incident occurs, the law changes or the auditors raise a point.
entries.t: An AI Use Policy for the Finance Function: What to Put in It

entries.q: What are AI guardrails in finance?
entries.a: AI guardrails are the rules and system settings that control what an AI tool can see and change, what is logged, and who must approve its output. In finance the core six are access by role, read-only by default, logging, data boundaries, human sign-off and testing.
entries.t: AI Guardrails for Finance Data: Access, Logging and Human Sign-Off

entries.q: Should AI tools have write access to the ERP?
entries.a: Not by default; start read-only and grant write access only as a separate, approved decision for specific transaction types. Keep a list of every tool with write rights and review it with your other access reviews.
entries.t: AI Guardrails for Finance Data: Access, Logging and Human Sign-Off

entries.q: What should be logged when finance uses AI?
entries.a: Log who asked, which documents and data the tool used, what it produced, and whether the output was accepted, changed or rejected. Keep logs for at least the audit cycle and confirm they can be retrieved.
entries.t: AI Guardrails for Finance Data: Access, Logging and Human Sign-Off

entries.q: What is the NIST AI Risk Management Framework?
entries.a: It is a voluntary framework released by NIST on 26 January 2023, organised around four functions: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. NIST added a Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) on 26 July 2024.
entries.t: AI Guardrails for Finance Data: Access, Logging and Human Sign-Off

entries.q: How do you stop finance data going into unapproved AI tools?
entries.a: Classify finance data, match each class to the tools approved for it, and make the approved route easier than the unapproved one. Bank details, payroll and unreleased results should be allowed only in tools approved for restricted data.
entries.t: AI Guardrails for Finance Data: Access, Logging and Human Sign-Off

entries.q: What does AI with company context mean?
entries.a: It means an AI tool that answers from your organization's own definitions, policies, chart of accounts, approval matrix and past decisions, rather than from general knowledge. The tool looks up approved documents when a question is asked and cites where the answer came from.
entries.t: AI With Company Context: The Layer Most Rollouts Skip

entries.q: Do we need to train our own AI model on company data?
entries.a: No, for most finance use cases the tool can look up approved documents at the time of each question instead. That keeps sources current, lets permissions apply per user, and means each answer can point to the document behind it.
entries.t: AI With Company Context: The Layer Most Rollouts Skip

entries.q: How do you stop an AI assistant showing people data they should not see?
entries.a: Make permissions follow the user, enforced by the system rather than by instructions to the model. If a person cannot open a document or a ledger, the assistant should not be able to use it to answer them.
entries.t: AI With Company Context: The Layer Most Rollouts Skip

entries.q: Can an AI assistant give accurate financial figures?
entries.a: Only if the figures are read from the ledger or reporting system and traced back to transactions. The model should explain numbers taken from the system of record, not produce them itself.
entries.t: AI With Company Context: The Layer Most Rollouts Skip

entries.q: What company context should a finance team prepare first?
entries.a: Start with the documents that answer the questions one team asks most, usually the approval matrix, the coding guide with account descriptions, and the expense and capitalisation policies. Resolve contradictions before loading them.
entries.t: AI With Company Context: The Layer Most Rollouts Skip

entries.q: Why does giving employees a general AI chatbot not change much?
entries.a: A general chatbot does not know the company's definitions, policies or data, so people use it for drafting and summarising rather than for the processes that drive cost and risk. The time savings stay with individuals and the way work gets done stays the same.
entries.t: Enterprise AI Adoption: Why Giving Everyone a Chatbot Is Not a Strategy

entries.q: What does enterprise AI adoption require?
entries.a: Enterprise AI adoption requires company context, use cases defined for each role, guardrails on data and review, and measurement of the process before and after. Licences and general training on their own do not change how work is done.
entries.t: Enterprise AI Adoption: Why Giving Everyone a Chatbot Is Not a Strategy

entries.q: Should the CFO own AI governance?
entries.a: Not always, but the CFO should have a formal say, because AI touches the data, approvals and controls finance runs. In Deloitte's Q2 2026 CFO Signals survey, 19% of CFOs said they have greatest responsibility for AI governance.
entries.t: Enterprise AI Adoption: Why Giving Everyone a Chatbot Is Not a Strategy

entries.q: How do you measure whether AI adoption is working?
entries.a: Measure the process, not tool usage: cycle time, exception rates, rework and hours put to other use, against a baseline taken before the change. Usage figures show only that people opened the tool.
entries.t: Enterprise AI Adoption: Why Giving Everyone a Chatbot Is Not a Strategy

entries.q: Where should a company start with AI beyond a chatbot?
entries.a: Start with one role and one high-volume, rules-heavy process, give the tool the company context it needs, set a named review step, and measure the result before extending to the next role.
entries.t: Enterprise AI Adoption: Why Giving Everyone a Chatbot Is Not a Strategy

entries.q: What is a compliance calendar?
entries.a: A compliance calendar is a schedule of every statutory filing and payment a group owes, by entity and jurisdiction, with due dates, owners and status. For multi-country groups it works best built on an obligations register rather than a spreadsheet.
entries.t: A Compliance Calendar for Multi-Country Groups: Why Spreadsheets Fail at Ten Jurisdictions

entries.q: Why do spreadsheet compliance calendars fail?
entries.a: They fail at scale because status is self-reported, evidence is stored elsewhere, nothing escalates automatically, copies drift apart and rule changes reach the file late.
entries.t: A Compliance Calendar for Multi-Country Groups: Why Spreadsheets Fail at Ten Jurisdictions

entries.q: What should an obligations register include?
entries.a: At minimum the entity, the obligation, the legal source, the due-date rule, the preparer, reviewer and approver, the payment step, the evidence required and the date the source was last checked.
entries.t: A Compliance Calendar for Multi-Country Groups: Why Spreadsheets Fail at Ten Jurisdictions

entries.q: How should compliance deadlines be escalated?
entries.a: On a written ladder tied to working days before the due date, moving from the preparer to the team lead, the country head and the CFO, so a late item reaches someone with authority in time.
entries.t: A Compliance Calendar for Multi-Country Groups: Why Spreadsheets Fail at Ten Jurisdictions

entries.q: How do you keep a compliance calendar current when rules change?
entries.a: Link every line to its official source, review sources on a schedule, log each change with its effective date and approver, and ask local advisers to confirm the register in writing each quarter.
entries.t: A Compliance Calendar for Multi-Country Groups: Why Spreadsheets Fail at Ten Jurisdictions

entries.q: Can AI manage statutory compliance?
entries.a: No, AI can watch sources, suggest which obligations a change affects and draft reminders, but people must verify changes against official sources and approve every filing.
entries.t: A Compliance Calendar for Multi-Country Groups: Why Spreadsheets Fail at Ten Jurisdictions

entries.q: What is the difference between financial and operational KPIs?
entries.a: Financial KPIs measure results recorded in the ledger, such as margin, DSO and cash conversion, while operational KPIs measure the activity that drives them, such as utilisation, on-time delivery and pipeline coverage.
entries.t: Financial and Operational KPIs in One View: What the ERP Cannot Give You

entries.q: Why can't the ERP report operational KPIs?
entries.a: The ERP records transactions with a financial effect, and most operational data sits in the CRM, HR and payroll, timesheet and operations systems. Combining them needs a layer above the ERP with agreed definitions.
entries.t: Financial and Operational KPIs in One View: What the ERP Cannot Give You

entries.q: Who should own KPI definitions?
entries.a: Finance should usually own the definitions register and the calculation, with a named metric owner in the business for each KPI and a system owner for each data source.
entries.t: Financial and Operational KPIs in One View: What the ERP Cannot Give You

entries.q: How many KPIs should a management team track?
entries.a: A short list, typically a few financial measures each paired with the operational KPIs that drive them. More than that tends to dilute attention in the monthly review.
entries.t: Financial and Operational KPIs in One View: What the ERP Cannot Give You

entries.q: Can AI build a KPI dashboard on its own?
entries.a: No, AI can draft commentary, flag definition breaks and answer questions with sourced figures, but the definitions, owners and tolerances have to be agreed by people first.
entries.t: Financial and Operational KPIs in One View: What the ERP Cannot Give You

entries.q: How do you consolidate entities that use different ERPs?
entries.a: Map each entity's local accounts to a single group chart in a mapping layer outside the ERPs, translate at group rates, then eliminate intercompany items. The ERPs stay as they are.
entries.t: Multi-Entity Reporting Across Different ERPs, Without a Data Warehouse Project

entries.q: Do I need a data warehouse for multi-entity reporting?
entries.a: Not for financial consolidation in most mid-sized groups. Read-only connectors to each ERP plus a governed mapping layer give a group view sooner, and a warehouse can follow when operational analytics need it.
entries.t: Multi-Entity Reporting Across Different ERPs, Without a Data Warehouse Project

entries.q: What is a mapping layer in consolidation?
entries.a: It is the set of rules that converts each entity's local trial balance into the group chart of accounts and segments, with effective dates and a change log, held outside the source systems.
entries.t: Multi-Entity Reporting Across Different ERPs, Without a Data Warehouse Project

entries.q: Who should own the chart of accounts mapping?
entries.a: Group reporting should own it, with entity controllers proposing changes and a second person approving each change before it affects a reporting pack.
entries.t: Multi-Entity Reporting Across Different ERPs, Without a Data Warehouse Project

entries.q: What intercompany items need to be eliminated?
entries.a: Intercompany balances, intercompany revenue and cost, dividends within the group, the parent's investment against subsidiary equity, and unrealised profit on goods still held inside the group.
entries.t: Multi-Entity Reporting Across Different ERPs, Without a Data Warehouse Project

entries.q: Should we wait for an ERP migration before fixing group reporting?
entries.a: No, a mapping layer can run on the current systems and survives a migration, because only the migrating entity needs to be remapped.
entries.t: Multi-Entity Reporting Across Different ERPs, Without a Data Warehouse Project

entries.q: What is intercompany reconciliation?
entries.a: Intercompany reconciliation is the process of agreeing the balances and transactions that entities in the same group record with each other, so they eliminate cleanly on consolidation.
entries.t: Intercompany Reconciliation: Why It Breaks Across Entities and Systems

entries.q: Why don't intercompany balances match?
entries.a: They usually differ because of timing, exchange rates, different charts of accounts, different ERPs or postings made by one side alone. Most differences become explainable once both sides use a shared reference and a common booking rule.
entries.t: Intercompany Reconciliation: Why It Breaks Across Entities and Systems

entries.q: Should intercompany matching use group currency or transaction currency?
entries.a: Match in transaction currency. Group currency adds differences caused only by the rates each entity used, which hides real exceptions among false ones.
entries.t: Intercompany Reconciliation: Why It Breaks Across Entities and Systems

entries.q: Can AI do intercompany matching on its own?
entries.a: No, AI can suggest matches and explain differences, but a person should accept any match that leads to a posting. Models can pair unrelated items that share an amount.
entries.t: Intercompany Reconciliation: Why It Breaks Across Entities and Systems

entries.q: What is collections prioritization?
entries.a: Collections prioritization is the daily decision about which customers to contact first, based on the amount at stake, the risk of non-payment and the likelihood that a contact will produce cash.
entries.t: Collections Prioritization: Who to Call First, and Why the Aging Report Gets It Wrong

entries.q: Why is the aging report not enough to prioritize collections?
entries.a: The aging report ranks balances by time alone. It ignores amount, payment trend, promise history and disputes, so it tends to focus effort on old, small or disputed items while new risks in large accounts wait.
entries.t: Collections Prioritization: Who to Call First, and Why the Aging Report Gets It Wrong

entries.q: What factors should be used to prioritize collections?
entries.a: Amount past due from the due date, changes in payment behavior, promise history, dispute status, credit risk and customer importance. Disputed items should leave the call list and go to an owner who can resolve them.
entries.t: Collections Prioritization: Who to Call First, and Why the Aging Report Gets It Wrong

entries.q: How often should a collections worklist be updated?
entries.a: Daily for the ranking, because payments, promises and disputes change every day. Review the method itself monthly against what was actually collected.
entries.t: Collections Prioritization: Who to Call First, and Why the Aging Report Gets It Wrong

entries.q: Can AI prioritize collections?
entries.a: AI can rank accounts daily from ledger data and collector notes, summarize an account before a call and draft reminders for review. Credit holds, payment plans and sensitive customer conversations should stay with people.
entries.t: Collections Prioritization: Who to Call First, and Why the Aging Report Gets It Wrong

entries.q: What is unapplied cash?
entries.a: Unapplied cash is a customer payment that has been received but not yet matched to the invoices it pays. It sits on the customer's account or in suspense until someone identifies what it settles.
entries.t: Unapplied Cash and Short Payments: The Quiet Drag on DSO

entries.q: Does unapplied cash affect DSO?
entries.a: Yes, and the direction depends on where it sits. Cash in suspense outside receivables overstates DSO, while cash held on account can leave paid invoices showing as past due.
entries.t: Unapplied Cash and Short Payments: The Quiet Drag on DSO

entries.q: What is the difference between a short payment and a deduction?
entries.a: A short payment is any payment below the invoice amount, and a deduction is a short payment taken for a stated reason such as a promotion, return or penalty. Both leave a balance that needs a decision.
entries.t: Unapplied Cash and Short Payments: The Quiet Drag on DSO

entries.q: Who should own unapplied cash?
entries.a: Each type should have one owner: cash application for unidentified payments, the collector for unexplained short payments, and whoever can judge validity for deductions. Finance sets deadlines and reviews the aging at each close.
entries.t: Unapplied Cash and Short Payments: The Quiet Drag on DSO

entries.q: Can AI do cash application?
entries.a: AI can reliably read remittances and propose matches, including multi-invoice payments, for a person to accept. Decisions that change what the customer owes should stay with a person.
entries.t: Unapplied Cash and Short Payments: The Quiet Drag on DSO

entries.q: How can a tax firm offer client advisory services?
entries.a: A tax firm can offer client advisory services by adding a year-round tier above the return: a daily view of the client's numbers, a mid-year review and a year-end planning call, delivered from the client's books. Software such as Navigator provides the client-facing layer, and a delivery partner can take on close and forecasting work.
entries.t: How Tax and Bookkeeping Firms Can Add Client Advisory Services With Navigator

entries.q: How do bookkeeping firms upsell advisory services?
entries.a: Start with clients who already ask questions between closes, run more than one company or carry a bank loan. Show them their own numbers in a daily view, then offer a tier that adds budget against actuals, a cash forecast and a monthly call to the close you already deliver.
entries.t: How Tax and Bookkeeping Firms Can Add Client Advisory Services With Navigator

entries.q: What does Navigator cost for accounting firms?
entries.a: Navigator lists at $299 a month for one entity and Navigator Pro at $499, with each additional entity at half price. Partner firms on the deliver model pay 25% off list, with a further 20% off for annual billing, and set their own client price.
entries.t: How Tax and Bookkeeping Firms Can Add Client Advisory Services With Navigator

entries.q: Can a CPA firm accept referral revenue from Navigator?
entries.a: It depends on the client and the state. The AICPA Code prohibits commissions for recommending products to clients for whom the firm performs attest work, and requires disclosure for other clients. Check your state board's rules, which can be stricter, before using the refer model.
entries.t: How Tax and Bookkeeping Firms Can Add Client Advisory Services With Navigator

entries.q: Does Navigator replace the bookkeeper or the CPA?
entries.a: No. Navigator reads the books read-only and explains them. It does not keep the books, close the month, prepare returns or provide assurance.
entries.t: How Tax and Bookkeeping Firms Can Add Client Advisory Services With Navigator

entries.q: Can Navigator run under our firm's brand?
entries.a: Your firm leads and Navigator is co-branded behind you. On the deliver model your firm invoices the client, who does not see a Navigator bill. It is not white-labelled.
entries.t: How Tax and Bookkeeping Firms Can Add Client Advisory Services With Navigator

entries.q: What is vendor master data?
entries.a: Vendor master data is the record the ERP holds for each supplier: name, address, tax ID, payment terms, payment method and bank details. The payment run uses it to decide where money goes.
entries.t: Vendor Master Data Controls: The Weak Point Behind Payment Fraud

entries.q: How should a company verify a vendor bank detail change?
entries.a: Call the supplier on a phone number already on file, not one supplied in the request, confirm the new details with a known contact, and record the call before the change takes effect.
entries.t: Vendor Master Data Controls: The Weak Point Behind Payment Fraud

entries.q: What segregation of duties is needed for vendor master data?
entries.a: The person who creates or changes vendor records should not also post invoices or release payments. Where a small team cannot separate those roles, an independent review of every change compensates.
entries.t: Vendor Master Data Controls: The Weak Point Behind Payment Fraud

entries.q: Why block dormant vendors?
entries.a: Dormant vendor records can be reactivated and paid with little scrutiny. Blocking them, and treating reactivation like a new vendor set-up, closes that route.
entries.t: Vendor Master Data Controls: The Weak Point Behind Payment Fraud

entries.q: Can AI detect vendor bank detail fraud?
entries.a: AI can flag patterns that often accompany it, such as a bank change followed quickly by a payment or one account shared by two vendors. It cannot verify the account; a person still makes the call-back.
entries.t: Vendor Master Data Controls: The Weak Point Behind Payment Fraud

entries.q: What causes duplicate payments in accounts payable?
entries.a: Duplicate payments are usually caused by the same invoice being keyed twice with small differences, by duplicate vendor records, by manual payments that are not linked to the invoice, or by mishandled credit memos and reversals.
entries.t: Duplicate Payments: How They Happen and the Controls That Catch Them

entries.q: Why does the ERP's duplicate invoice check not stop every duplicate?
entries.a: It does not, because it looks for an exact match on a fixed set of fields. A reference keyed differently or a second vendor record is enough to pass it.
entries.t: Duplicate Payments: How They Happen and the Controls That Catch Them

entries.q: What is the difference between preventive and detective controls for duplicate payments?
entries.a: A preventive control stops a duplicate invoice from being posted or paid, while a detective control finds it afterwards. The most useful detective control reviews the payment proposal for near-matches before the money leaves.
entries.t: Duplicate Payments: How They Happen and the Controls That Catch Them

entries.q: What is fuzzy matching for duplicate invoices?
entries.a: Fuzzy matching scores pairs of invoices on how similar they are across reference, amount, date, vendor and bank account, rather than requiring an exact match. Recurring payments need separate treatment or they produce false alarms.
entries.t: Duplicate Payments: How They Happen and the Controls That Catch Them

entries.q: How do you recover a duplicate payment?
entries.a: Ask the vendor for a refund or agree an offset against the next invoice, and confirm it in writing. Then trace which control failed and fix it.
entries.t: Duplicate Payments: How They Happen and the Controls That Catch Them

entries.q: What is a three-way match exception?
entries.a: A three-way match exception is an invoice that does not agree with its purchase order and goods receipt on price, quantity or receipt, so the ERP blocks it for payment until someone resolves the difference.
entries.t: Three-Way Match Exceptions: Why They Pile Up and What Clears Them

entries.q: What causes most three-way match exceptions?
entries.a: Usually timing and data rather than vendor error: late goods receipts, tolerances that do not fit, unconfirmed service orders, partial deliveries and unit-of-measure differences.
entries.t: Three-Way Match Exceptions: Why They Pile Up and What Clears Them

entries.q: Who should resolve a price variance on an invoice?
entries.a: The buyer or procurement owner should resolve a price variance, because accepting a different price is a purchasing decision. AP should send it with the evidence and track the answer.
entries.t: Three-Way Match Exceptions: Why They Pile Up and What Clears Them

entries.q: Should we widen tolerances to reduce exceptions?
entries.a: Only after you know which exceptions the tolerance causes and what a wider one would let through. The controller should make and document that decision.
entries.t: Three-Way Match Exceptions: Why They Pile Up and What Clears Them

entries.q: Can AI release blocked invoices automatically?
entries.a: In our view it should not. Releasing a block is a decision for a person with the authority to make it; AI prepares the evidence.
entries.t: Three-Way Match Exceptions: Why They Pile Up and What Clears Them

entries.q: What is management by exception in finance?
entries.a: It is a way of designing finance work so that rules handle routine items and people see only the items that fall outside those rules. Each exception has a reason, a named owner, a visible age and a defined escalation path.
entries.t: Management by Exception in Finance: Designing Work Around What Needs a Person

entries.q: How should exception thresholds be set?
entries.a: Use value thresholds for routine variances and risk rules for events that always need a person, such as changed supplier bank details or a new supplier. Review thresholds against the monthly exception rate by reason code.
entries.t: Management by Exception in Finance: Designing Work Around What Needs a Person

entries.q: Who should own a finance exception?
entries.a: One named person per exception type, who may sit outside finance where the cause does, such as a buyer for price variances. Shared inboxes without a named owner are where exceptions age.
entries.t: Management by Exception in Finance: Designing Work Around What Needs a Person

entries.q: How does AI support management by exception?
entries.a: AI sorts items into matched, nearly matched and unmatched, and gathers the facts a person needs to decide each exception. A person still approves anything that releases cash or changes master data.
entries.t: Management by Exception in Finance: Designing Work Around What Needs a Person

entries.q: What is the main risk of management by exception?
entries.a: Items that clear automatically are not looked at by anyone. Regular sampling of auto-cleared items and an annual review of thresholds reduce the chance that errors or fraud sit unseen below the line.
entries.t: Management by Exception in Finance: Designing Work Around What Needs a Person

entries.q: What do high-growth accounting firms do differently?
entries.a: They sell client advisory as a defined, recurring, fixed-fee service, meet clients more often than once a year, specialise in industry niches and move production work off their senior people. Each of these shows up in the 2024 CAS Benchmark Survey or Thomson Reuters' tax firm research.
entries.t: What High-Growth Accounting Firms Get Right: Client Advisory

entries.q: How fast are client accounting and advisory services growing?
entries.a: The AICPA and CPA.com 2024 CAS Benchmark Survey reported median CAS growth of 17% across 206 practices for 2023, against a 9.11% median increase in total firm net client fees in the 2023 MAP survey.
entries.t: What High-Growth Accounting Firms Get Right: Client Advisory

entries.q: What percentage of accounting firms offer advisory services?
entries.a: Wolters Kluwer's 2025 survey found 94% of US firms offer advisory services. But in the 2024 CAS Benchmark Survey, 39% of CAS practices said they do not offer business insights services, and fewer than one-third earned more than 10% of CAS revenue from them.
entries.t: What High-Growth Accounting Firms Get Right: Client Advisory

entries.q: How should accounting firms price advisory services?
entries.a: Most growing practices use fixed fees payable monthly, quarterly or annually. In the 2024 CAS Benchmark Survey, 84% of respondents were shifting to fixed-fee billing and only 10% still billed mainly by the hour.
entries.t: What High-Growth Accounting Firms Get Right: Client Advisory

entries.q: How often should accountants meet clients to grow advisory?
entries.a: At least quarterly. In Thomson Reuters' 2026 tax firm advisory report, 83% of firms with quarterly client touchpoints had proactively offered advisory services, against 52% and 58% for firms meeting clients once or twice a year.
entries.t: What High-Growth Accounting Firms Get Right: Client Advisory

entries.q: What is financial storytelling in accounting?
entries.a: Financial storytelling is explaining a client's financial results as what changed, why it changed and what to do about it, in business language rather than ledger language, so the numbers lead to a decision.
entries.t: From Data to Decisions: Finding the Story in the Numbers

entries.q: How do you explain financial statements to a business owner?
entries.a: Start with the decision they face, highlight the two or three movements that bear on it, explain each by its business driver such as price, volume or labor efficiency, and end with one recommended action. Keep the full statements behind it as backup.
entries.t: From Data to Decisions: Finding the Story in the Numbers

entries.q: What should monthly variance commentary include?
entries.a: A one-line headline, the movements above an agreed materiality threshold with their drivers, what those movements mean for the decisions ahead, one recommendation and one risk to watch.
entries.t: From Data to Decisions: Finding the Story in the Numbers

entries.q: How do you decide which variances to explain?
entries.a: Set a threshold that combines a percentage and a dollar amount, compare against the baseline that matches the decision, such as budget, prior year or a trailing average, and limit the commentary to two or three items.
entries.t: From Data to Decisions: Finding the Story in the Numbers

entries.q: Can software write variance commentary?
entries.a: Software can find and quantify the movements and draft a plain-language explanation from the ledger. Deciding what matters to this owner, and what to recommend, still sits with the accountant.
entries.t: From Data to Decisions: Finding the Story in the Numbers

entries.q: What are the most common AI use cases in finance?
entries.a: The most common, according to a Gartner release from November 2025 based on 183 CFOs and senior finance leaders, were knowledge management (49%), AP process automation (37%) and error and anomaly detection (34%). Reconciliation matching and cash application also tend to score well on volume and rules.
entries.t: AI Use Cases in Finance: How to Rank Them by Volume, Rules and Risk

entries.q: Which finance process should a CFO apply AI to first?
entries.a: Start with a process that has high volume, clear written rules and structured data, where a person already reviews the exceptions. Invoice coding, reconciliation matching and pre-payment duplicate checks usually qualify.
entries.t: AI Use Cases in Finance: How to Rank Them by Volume, Rules and Risk

entries.q: How do you prioritize AI use cases in finance?
entries.a: Score each use case from 1 to 5 on volume, rule-bound work, data availability, error cost and control risk. Rank by the benefit total, then use the risk total to decide how much human approval the design needs.
entries.t: AI Use Cases in Finance: How to Rank Them by Volume, Rules and Risk

entries.q: Should AI write board commentary?
entries.a: Not as a first project. Board narrative is low in volume, has no fixed rules and carries a high cost when wrong, so it ranks low on benefit and high on risk. AI drafting with careful human editing can come later.
entries.t: AI Use Cases in Finance: How to Rank Them by Volume, Rules and Risk

entries.q: What makes a finance process a poor fit for AI?
entries.a: Low volume, rules that live in people's heads, data that is scattered or inconsistent, and a high cost if an error goes unnoticed. Processes with these features need fixing or documenting before AI adds much.
entries.t: AI Use Cases in Finance: How to Rank Them by Volume, Rules and Risk

entries.q: How do you measure finance team capacity?
entries.a: Log hours by process in half-hour blocks for four weeks, tag each block as first-pass, rework or interruption, and pull transaction volumes for the same period from the system. Hours per unit and rework share by process then show where capacity goes.
entries.t: Finance Team Capacity: A Time Audit of Where the Hours Go

entries.q: How long should a finance time audit run?
entries.a: Four weeks, including one full month-end close. That captures the routine weeks and the close peak without wearing the team out.
entries.t: Finance Team Capacity: A Time Audit of Where the Hours Go

entries.q: Which finance processes are best suited to AI?
entries.a: Processes with high volume, written rules and low rework come first, such as bank matching and standard invoice coding. Where rework is high, fix its upstream cause first, or automation only moves exceptions faster.
entries.t: Finance Team Capacity: A Time Audit of Where the Hours Go

entries.q: What does it typically cost to process a supplier invoice?
entries.a: APQC's Open Standards Benchmarking puts the cross-industry median at $6.50 per invoice processed, across 6,546 companies. Your figure depends on how you allocate people and system costs, so track your own trend before comparing.
entries.t: Finance Team Capacity: A Time Audit of Where the Hours Go
